# Public Datasets

## ResStock 2025 Release 1 New

The updated dataset builds on the End Use Savings Shapes methodology, with 28 packages. New major updates include the additions of Hawaii and Alaska, electric vehicles, updated utility rates, HVAC demand flexibility, electric panel estimations, and improved geothermal heat pump modeling. For details about the ResStock model used to create this dataset, see the Technical Reference Guide and the short readme paper which has a description of all packages, important assumptions, and changes from the last dataset release. A summary of how column names have changed in this dataset since 2024 Release 2 is also available. The geothermal heat pump results from this AMY 2018 2025 Release 1 dataset are shown in the Evaluating Geothermal Performance for the U.S. Building Stock Tableau dashboard with ComStock geothermal heat pump results.

For more information on this dataset, and other ResStock datasets, see our User Resource Website which has examples, FAQs, measure documentation and more. Have additional questions or comments? Email our team at ResStock@nlr.gov.

### ResStock 2025 Release 1

The measure packages included in this release include:

  1. Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
  2. Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
  3. Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
  4. Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
  5. Dual Fuel Heat Pump
  6. Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
  7. Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER)
  8. Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER)
  9. Heat Pump Water Heater
  10. Natural Gas Water Heater
  11. Advanced Air Sealing
  12. Attic Floor Insulation
  13. Duct Sealing and Insulation
  14. Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation

Improved air source heat pump modeling 
The variable speed air-source heat pump model in the 2025.1 release uses performance data 
derived from the NEEP database to describe how it operates. These data include capacity and 
COP values at minimum and maximum compressor speeds and various outdoor temperatures.  
 
This release also introduces the ability to restrict the sizing of heat pumps to what the baseline 
duct size allows. This reflects a scenario where an occupant installs a heat pump into an existing 
household but does not expand or retrofit the duct system. This sizing restriction is used with the 
cold climate air-source heat pump model in the 2025.1 release. 
 
Improved geothermal heat pump modeling 
New models of different types of geothermal heat pumps (GHPs), including two stage and 
variable speed equipment, are included in the latest release. Scenarios modeled include single-
stage, two-stage, and variable speed GHP. Two-stage GHPs make up the majority of the market 
today, and a scenario of a two-stage GHP plus envelope improvements was also included in this 
release. The workflow now takes advantage of different EnergyPlus objects designed for 
modeling variable speed equipment more explicitly.  
 
Other housing characteristics updates 
As a result of Alaska and Hawaii integration, several baseline housing characteristics are 
updated. Notably, secondary heating is modeled for Alaskan homes, water heaters now include 
solar thermal (mostly in Hawaii), pool heaters now include heat pump heaters, and rooftop PV 
saturation (modeled for single-family detached only) has been updated from 2018 level to 2023 
per EIA 861 reporting.

## Usage

The `sdr_option_application_report.csv` file can be used for:

  1. Error Detection: It helps catch errors by flagging when options are applied to zero buildings, which indicates a problem in the upgrade specification. The CI job automatically checks for this and fails if there are any option with zero applicability.

  2. Upgrade Documentation: It documents in tabular form which specific options were applied in each upgrade.

  3. Applicability Analysis: It shows how widely each upgrade and options are applied across the building stock.

  4. Reporting: It provides key applicability statistics for use in measure documentation.

## Creation

`sdr_option_application_report.csv` file is automatically created by ResStock CI job. The CI uses the `upgrades_analyzer` tool in buildstock-query with the `project_national/sdr_upgrades_tmy3.yml` and a fresh 550K sample as input to generate this file. Whenever the yaml apply logic or the housing characteristics changes, the CI job will regenerate this file and commit to the repo.

# ResStock

Project Website: https://resstock.nlr.gov/ 
Performer: National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) – Golden, CO
Performance Period: 2014 –
DOE Funding:
Related Projects: OpenStudio, Scout

#### Project Objective

Traditional stock models are coarse grain, often relying on a few prototype models to represent a single building type in a single climate zone. For some analyses, such coarse granularity can average out relevant details and return “all-or-nothing” results that miss significant opportunities. ResStock is a multi-resolution residential stock modeling framework. ResStock combines data from multiple sources including the EIA’s Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) to create high-resolution conditional probability tables for home characteristics like square footage, insulation, window-type, HVAC type, and HVAC efficiency. ResStock then uses sampling to generate a statistically representative set of models for the desired region. ResStock leverages OpenStudio to create the models and run them.

## ResStock 2025 Release 1 New

The updated dataset builds on the End Use Savings Shapes methodology, with 28 packages. New major updates include the additions of Hawaii and Alaska, electric vehicles, updated utility rates, HVAC demand flexibility, electric panel estimations, and improved geothermal heat pump modeling. Improved air source heat pump modeling 
The variable speed air-source heat pump model in the 2025.1 release uses performance data 
derived from the NEEP database to describe how it operates. These data include capacity and 
COP values at minimum and maximum compressor speeds and various outdoor temperatures.  
 
This release also introduces the ability to restrict the sizing of heat pumps to what the baseline 
duct size allows. This reflects a scenario where an occupant installs a heat pump into an existing 
household but does not expand or retrofit the duct system. This sizing restriction is used with the 
cold climate air-source heat pump model in the 2025.1 release. 
 
Improved geothermal heat pump modeling 
New models of different types of geothermal heat pumps (GHPs), including two stage and 
variable speed equipment, are included in the latest release. Scenarios modeled include single-
stage, two-stage, and variable speed GHP. Two-stage GHPs make up the majority of the market 
today, and a scenario of a two-stage GHP plus envelope improvements was also included in this 
release. The workflow now takes advantage of different EnergyPlus objects designed for 
modeling variable speed equipment more explicitly.  
 
Other housing characteristics updates 
As a result of Alaska and Hawaii integration, several baseline housing characteristics are 
updated. Notably, secondary heating is modeled for Alaskan homes, water heaters now include 
solar thermal (mostly in Hawaii), pool heaters now include heat pump heaters, and rooftop PV 
saturation (modeled for single-family detached only) has been updated from 2018 level to 2023 
per EIA 861 reporting.

The following table summarizes the new upgrade measures introduced in this dataset release. All 
upgrade measures in this release are considered new. Throughout ResStock documentation, the

  * The first option within this upgrade changes “HVAC Heating Efficiency” to “ASHP, SEER 16, 9.2 HSPF”

  * This option was applied to 408,859 buildings, representing 74.3% of the total stock of 550,000 buildings.

  * The special option_num “-1” with option “All” shows the total applicability of the entire upgrade package. This is used to calculate the total applicability of the entire upgrade package and is not a real option in the project yaml file.

## Usage

The `sdr_option_application_report.csv` file can be used for:

  1. Error Detection: It helps catch errors by flagging when options are applied to zero buildings, which indicates a problem in the upgrade specification. The CI job automatically checks for this and fails if there are any option with zero applicability.

  2. Upgrade Documentation: It documents in tabular form which specific options were applied in each upgrade.

  3. Applicability Analysis: It shows how widely each upgrade and options are applied across the building stock.

  4. Reporting: It provides key applicability statistics for use in measure documentation.

## Creation

`sdr_option_application_report.csv` file is automatically created by ResStock CI job. The CI uses the `upgrades_analyzer` tool in buildstock-query with the `project_national/sdr_upgrades_tmy3.yml` and a fresh 550K sample as input to generate this file. Whenever the yaml apply logic or the housing characteristics changes, the CI job will regenerate this file and commit to the repo.

# ResStock

Project Website: https://resstock.nlr.gov/ 
Performer: National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) – Golden, CO
Performance Period: 2014 –
DOE Funding:
Related Projects: OpenStudio, Scout

#### Project Objective

Traditional stock models are coarse grain, often relying on a few prototype models to represent a single building type in a single climate zone. For some analyses, such coarse granularity can average out relevant details and return “all-or-nothing” results that miss significant opportunities. ResStock is a multi-resolution residential stock modeling framework. ResStock combines data from multiple sources including the EIA’s Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) to create high-resolution conditional probability tables for home characteristics like square footage, insulation, window-type, HVAC type, and HVAC efficiency. ResStock then uses sampling to generate a statistically representative set of models for the desired region. ResStock leverages OpenStudio to create the models and run them.

We introduce NeuralBES (Building Energy Simulation), a differentiable emulator that resolves this tradeoff by parameterizing a resistance--capacitance (RC) based thermal model with a shared neural encoder: static building metadata such as floor area, vintage, and HVAC type is mapped to physically bounded capacitances, conductances, and equipment coefficients, which become the coefficients of a scalar linear recurrence solved via a log-space parallel scan, and a predictor--corrector loop closes the thermostat--temperature nonlinearity while preserving full-horizon gradient flow. L63@P5: The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact,
L64@P5: market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. “Measures” refers to retrofits that can be
L65@P5: applied to buildings during modeling.
L66@P5: An “end-use savings shape” is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building
L67@P5: and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It
L68@P5: results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas,
L69@P5: propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.
L70@P5: ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data
L71@P5: sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the
L72@P5: annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States.
L73@P5: The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018.
L74@P5: Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is
L75@P5: available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are
L76@P5: available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).
L77@P5: This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Heating, Ventilation,
L78@P5: and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) Load Flexibility.
L79@P5: The HVAC load flexibility measure modifies the heating and cooling thermostat set points
L80@P5: before peak periods to preheat or precool the building or during peak periods to shift load away
L81@P5: from peak periods. In real deployments of demand flexibility via smart thermostats, the dispatch
L82@P5: is typically limited to a handful of days per year to avoid customer fatigue. But the goal of this
L83@P5: modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical
L84@P5: potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is
L85@P5: dispatched nearly every day in the modeled dataset. Although the profile on any given day is
L86@P5: realistic, the full annual load profiles do not reflect the realistic dispatch of HVAC load
L87@P5: flexibility. Details on the appropriate use of the load profiles can be found in this document.
L88@P5: To keep the logic simple and to generate the most comprehensive result that can support
L89@P5: different future analysis, this measure applies to all dwelling units with either a heating or a
L90@P5: cooling system (approximately 99.7% of the dwelling units modeled in ResStock); however, the
L91@P5: heating load analysis in this document is done on only buildings with electric heating. With a 4°F
L92@P5: offset during the 4-hour peak periods across all 51 states, this resulted in an average reduction of
L93@P5: 57% in peak period heating electricity consumption during the winter months and a 54%
L94@P5-6: reduction in peak period cooling electricity during the summer months.vi

L192: This dataset describes the timeseries energy consumption of the U.S. residential building stock at the end-use level. L193: Two versions of this dataset have been created: one with actual weather data from 2018, and another with typical (TMY3) weather data. L62@P5: Executive Summary
L63@P5: The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact,
L64@P5: market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. “Measures” refers to retrofits that can be
L65@P5: applied to buildings during modeling.
L66@P5: An “end-use savings shape” is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building
L67@P5: and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It
L68@P5: results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas,
L69@P5: propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.
L70@P5: ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data
L71@P5: sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the
L72@P5: annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States.
L73@P5: The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018.
L74@P5: Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is
L75@P5: available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are
L76@P5: available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).
L77@P5: This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Heating, Ventilation,
L78@P5: and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) Load Flexibility.
L79@P5: The HVAC load flexibility measure modifies the heating and cooling thermostat set points
L80@P5: before peak periods to preheat or precool the building or during peak periods to shift load away
L81@P5: from peak periods. In real deployments of demand flexibility via smart thermostats, the dispatch
L82@P5: is typically limited to a handful of days per year to avoid customer fatigue. But the goal of this
L83@P5: modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical
L84@P5: potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is
L85@P5: dispatched nearly every day in the modeled dataset. Although the profile on any given day is
L86@P5: realistic, the full annual load profiles do not reflect the realistic dispatch of HVAC load
L87@P5: flexibility. Details on the appropriate use of the load profiles can be found in this document.
L88@P5: To keep the logic simple and to generate the most comprehensive result that can support
L89@P5: different future analysis, this measure applies to all dwelling units with either a heating or a
L90@P5: cooling system (approximately 99.7% of the dwelling units modeled in ResStock); however, the
L91@P5: heating load analysis in this document is done on only buildings with electric heating. With a 4°F
L92@P5: offset during the 4-hour peak periods across all 51 states, this resulted in an average reduction of
L93@P5: 57% in peak period heating electricity consumption during the winter months and a 54%
L94@P5-6: reduction in peak period cooling electricity during the summer months.vi

L222@P9: Within the context of demand flexibility programs, the internet-connected feature of a smart
L223@P9: thermostat is used by the utility (with customer consent) to remotely adjust the thermostat set
L224@P9-10: points during target times. For example, Xcel Energy deploys Ecobee smart thermostats in their 3
L225@P10: This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
L226@P10: demand response program. These thermostats adjust customer home cooling set points by 1°F–
L227@P10: 4°F for up to 4 hours when there is a risk of an electricity shortage, as determined by Xcel
L228@P10: Energy.
L229@P10: 1.2 Technical Measure Details
L230@P10: Demand flexibility is commonly categorized into four groups: load shaping, load shifting, load
L231@P10: shedding, and load shimmying (Peter Alstone, 2017). In this analysis, we consider load shifting
L232@P10: and load shedding. In the following discussion, the peak period, or “on-peak window,” is the
L233@P10: window of time when the peak is to be reduced. The pre-peak window is the window of time
L234@P10: immediately preceding the peak period.
L235@P10: 1.2.1 Load Shifting
L236@P10: As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017), load shifting “represents DR [demand response] that
L237@P10: encourages the movement of energy consumption from times of high demand to times when
L238@P10: there is a surplus of renewable generation. Shift could smooth net load ramps associated with
L239@P10: daily patterns of solar energy generation.”
L240@P10: For this analysis, load shifting is accomplished by preheating (for heating days) or precooling
L241@P10: (for cooling days) the building prior to the on-peak window (during the pre-peak window). The
L242@P10: idea is that the preheating or precooling increases the load prior to the on-peak window,
L243@P10: conditions the indoor air, and preconditions the thermal mass and air in the building. Then the
L244@P10: building requires less heating or cooling energy to maintain the set point during the on-peak
L245@P10: window, reducing the overall load profile during this window. The extent of the load reduction
L246@P10: will depend on the building’s characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation,
L247@P10: the infiltration, the duration of the preconditioning, and the timing of the peak period.
L248@P10: 1.2.2 Load Shedding
L249@P10: As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017), load shedding “describes loads that can be curtailed to
L250@P10: provide peak capacity and support the system in emergency or contingency events.”
L251@P10: For this analysis, load shedding is accomplished by decreasing the heating set point and
L252@P10: increasing the cooling set point of the building during the on-peak window. This allows the
L253@P10: temperature to drift beyond the original set point during the on-peak window, trading decreased
L254@P10: thermal comfort for reduced peak load. How quickly the temperature drifts to the modified set
L255@P10: point will depend on the building’s characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of
L256@P10: insulation, and the infiltration.
L257@P10: 1.2.3 Set Point Change and Magnitude
L258@P10: Different durations of pre-peak load shifting and different set point offsets for load shifting or
L259@P10: load shedding can be applied by HVAC load flexibility programs. For a mild impact on
L260@P10: residents, a shorter on-peak duration (e.g., 2 hours) with a small set point offset during the onpeak hour (e.g., 2°F) can be used. In contrast, for the maximum load change, a longer pre-peak
L261@P10: period (e.g., 4 hours) with larger set point adjustments, such as a low precooling set point (e.g.,
L262@P10-11: 60°F) and/or a high on-peak cooling set point (e.g., 80°F), may be applied.4
L263@P11: This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.

L223@P9: thermostat is used by the utility (with customer consent) to remotely adjust the thermostat set
L224@P9-10: points during target times. For example, Xcel Energy deploys Ecobee smart thermostats in their 3

L229@P10: 1.2 Technical Measure Details
L230@P10: Demand flexibility is commonly categorized into four groups: load shaping, load shifting, load
L231@P10: shedding, and load shimmying (Peter Alstone, 2017). In this analysis, we consider load shifting
L232@P10: and load shedding. In the following discussion, the peak period, or “on-peak window,” is the
L233@P10: window of time when the peak is to be reduced. The pre-peak window is the window of time
L234@P10: immediately preceding the peak period.
L235@P10: 1.2.1 Load Shifting
L236@P10: As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017), load shifting “represents DR [demand response] that
L237@P10: encourages the movement of energy consumption from times of high demand to times when
L238@P10: there is a surplus of renewable generation. Shift could smooth net load ramps associated with
L239@P10: daily patterns of solar energy generation.”
L240@P10: For this analysis, load shifting is accomplished by preheating (for heating days) or precooling
L241@P10: (for cooling days) the building prior to the on-peak window (during the pre-peak window). The
L242@P10: idea is that the preheating or precooling increases the load prior to the on-peak window,
L243@P10: conditions the indoor air, and preconditions the thermal mass and air in the building. Then the
L244@P10: building requires less heating or cooling energy to maintain the set point during the on-peak
L245@P10: window, reducing the overall load profile during this window. The extent of the load reduction
L246@P10: will depend on the building’s characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation,
L247@P10: the infiltration, the duration of the preconditioning, and the timing of the peak period.
L248@P10: 1.2.2 Load Shedding
L249@P10: As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017), load shedding “describes loads that can be curtailed to
L250@P10: provide peak capacity and support the system in emergency or contingency events.”
L251@P10: For this analysis, load shedding is accomplished by decreasing the heating set point and
L252@P10: increasing the cooling set point of the building during the on-peak window. This allows the
L253@P10: temperature to drift beyond the original set point during the on-peak window, trading decreased
L254@P10: thermal comfort for reduced peak load. How quickly the temperature drifts to the modified set
L255@P10: point will depend on the building’s characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of
L256@P10: insulation, and the infiltration.
L257@P10: 1.2.3 Set Point Change and Magnitude
L258@P10: Different durations of pre-peak load shifting and different set point offsets for load shifting or
L259@P10: load shedding can be applied by HVAC load flexibility programs. For a mild impact on
L260@P10: residents, a shorter on-peak duration (e.g., 2 hours) with a small set point offset during the onpeak hour (e.g., 2°F) can be used. In contrast, for the maximum load change, a longer pre-peak
L261@P10: period (e.g., 4 hours) with larger set point adjustments, such as a low precooling set point (e.g.,
L262@P10-11: 60°F) and/or a high on-peak cooling set point (e.g., 80°F), may be applied.4

item.text:
The HVAC demand flexibility measures are **upgrades 24–28**. They differ in **when they change thermostat settings, the temperature offset, and the duration**. The official [2025 Release 1 package list](https://resstock.nlr.gov/datasets) identifies all five:

| Upgrade ID | Strategy | Before the peak period | During the peak period |
|---|---|---|---|
| **24** | Load shedding, 2°F | No preconditioning | Lower heating setpoint / raise cooling setpoint by **2°F for 4 hours** |
| **25** | Load shifting, 4 hours, 2°F | Preheat / precool by **2°F for 4 hours** | Return to normal thermostat settings |
| **26** | Load shedding, 4°F | No preconditioning | Lower heating setpoint / raise cooling setpoint by **4°F for 4 hours** |
| **27** | Load shifting, 4 hours, 4°F | Preheat / precool by **4°F for 4 hours** | Return to normal thermostat settings |
| **28** | Load shifting, 1 hour, 2°F | Preheat / precool by **2°F for 1 hour** | Return to normal thermostat settings |

The durations and offsets are confirmed in [HVAC Load Flexibility documentation, Table 8, p. 25](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf#page=33).

**Shedding** reduces HVAC demand during the peak by allowing indoor temperatures to drift farther from normal settings. **Shifting** runs heating or cooling beforehand, storing heat or cooling in the building so less is needed during the peak. The final release treats these as separate strategies; its shifting upgrades do **not** also apply an on-peak thermostat setback. The 4°F options use larger temperature changes; upgrade 28 uses shorter preconditioning than upgrade 25. [Technical explanation, §§1.2 and 4.4](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf).

I started with your [release index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NatLabRockies/buildstock-corpus/resstock_amy2018_2025_release_1-v1/processed/resstock/resstock_amy2018_2025_release_1/index.json), but its JSON contents did not render in the browsing tool, so I verified the comparison against the official sources above.
